review_text_raw:
"Cyber Manhunt" is a visual novel disguised as a detective game: it has a few timed puzzles and optional information, but in general the game is linear.
The story is far from perfect: it is too dark and not depressing enough at the same time to be realistic. The ending chapter is just meh. The gameplay has a few shortcomings: the in-game desktop is not responsive enough, the data gathering process is tedious, and the puzzles can be bothersome given the running timer. The stylization is fine, I guess, until it comes to anything computer-related (Of course, it is of little importance, but now I know that viruses are always written in C and bash while any database with private data utilizes systemd. Wait. What?) The English translation is sub-par and has lots of typos.
It is a bit sad, because I see the potential in this game, but I cannot recommend it.

review_text_raw:
I couldn't play it for longer than 30 minutes. It's a cool concept, hence why I picked the game up in a sale, but for a text-based game the language was horrible. The dialogue was stilted, forced, and in some cases grammatically incorrect. The developers do have a reasonably good command of English, but that does not mean that they can write believable and natural-sounding dialogue, and they've clearly foregone hiring a proofreader. 

I recommend Orwell, which is the same concept but with much better writing.

review_text_raw:
The mechanics are that of an uninspired phishing simulation. Which contrasts with the narrative framing of "you are a really dangerous nerd". I feel like a game like grayhack or hacknet is fit more for that framing. Even the tutorial was highly boring for me. Maybe the story you get after the tutorial is good, but i didn't get that far.

Well you see I understand that a game would need some embellishing and effects to sell the power fantasy and divert from the seams of skipping real life logic, but the choices this game made regarding that front makes me see those seams harder rather than immersing me in the fantasy.

very light spoilers ahead from the first ten minutes of gameplay(tutorial and intro)

First, i got whiplashed right off with the phrase "our company got a BILLION BYTES of customer data". Holy shit dude, that's a lot for a large tech company at the like 90s maybe. Not for the presented "everyone is glued to their phones using social media" setting.  Less than a god damn gigabyte, basically three times less than the space this game takes on your ssd.

Then we got the random code prompts opening every time we copy the details from the browser about someone's facebook account to some contacts type information collection software. It feels less hackery and more like the "linux users when x" memes, because why would code prompts open when you are just copy pasting something from one gui to some other gui.


Then apparently we have access to the data of almost all citizens in our nation through the company database software. For some reason when accessing the data we or the software executes almost totally unrelated linux commands, which i don't understand why since it is not a cli tool but poses as a professional corpo gui software, but i guess the company in the story fired the user interface designer/programmer before they finished their job.

Then there is the password "cracker" software. Except this game's version makes me feel like a loser script kiddie the most. All you do is fill in a bunch of details you gathered from the dude's social media page, and the "cracker" spits out some password guess with very few amount of characters based on the entered information. And somehow it's correct like it's some oracle.

It reminds me of that one CheeseParade skit where the guy goes "He's not a hacker, he's a password guesser", and then the guy proceeds to get locked out of the system for inputting the wrong password since it was a guess based on a whim.

Also the OS apparently can't handle a bunch of high speed showcase of cyber security news, crashes and has to restart, which felt like a funny unintentional commentary on the ram shortage crisis. That was the most fun part of the game for me. 

Anyways, so if you like an overly dressed up phishing simulator with seemingly nice worldbuilding and perhaps a good story if you ignore the technical knowledge shortcomings of the writers here and there, maybe its your thing, Otherwise, nah.

review_text_raw:
I was 80% of the way to giving this a thumbs because hey, it's ten bucks and it will kill a few hours of your life, the puzzles are somewhat challenging and clicking around playing pretend-hacker is always diverting.

It doesn't quite get over the finish line for a few reasons:

As much there are ominous warnings about sensitive subject matter and deep thoughts concerning your privacy, the game is REALLY rough from a narrative standpoint. The game is translated from Chinese, and while their English is a great deal better than my non-existent Mandarin, it's still not good, with really clunky dialogue that kills any emotional heft the story may be going for and some variable (but mostly bad) voice acting. And when you're tackling serious topics like sexual assault and bullying and online harassment and such, you shouldn't be giggling at deadpan "he attacked me like an animal" deliveries. In other words, don't expect to lose yourself in the story here.

But whatever, it's a budget game, they couldn't shell out for a localization team, that's forgivable. You can still have a good time playing pretend-hacker and solving puzzles, right?

Well... you could have, maybe, if the game weren't so full of bugs. Some are merely annoying, like someone asking you over the phone the name they used when they e-mailed you and you put in that name and they say it's wrong, so you double-check and look for one of the two other options there, but you don't see it, so you throw your hands up, look at a guide, see the answer, look again at the e-mail wondering where they ever used the name and then just put it in because you've already wasted ten minutes and just want to get on with it. Someone quizzes you on what part of their body was injured, and that information was never made available anywhere. You can try these puzzles repeatedly, but you can't back out if you fail and go double-check stuff again, you have to go all the way out to the main menu and then re-continue the game.

None of this was enough to turn me off the game until I hit Chapter 5. Without going into details, Chapter 5 was so buggy, it forced me to quit and re-load the game three times, and finally reached a point where I really couldn't progress because a specific tool I needed to finish a puzzle wouldn't load. By that point, I was done.

What inevitably earns this game the thumbs down is just that there are much better hacking games and "surveillance is bad" games out there. TIS-100, Hacknet, Grey Hack, Orwell. Even if this game is cheaper, go spend the extra money elsewhere. It will be worth it.
